title: Turbans, not helmets
hook: Sikh soldiers kept their turbans instead of steel helmets

segments.voice: Yesterday, the trenches, and your line was far from punjab. Did you thank someone who served? Today we stay at the front, and look at what the soldiers wore on their heads. Day nine hundred ninety-eight.

Two things on a table. One is a steel helmet, round and heavy, the kind armies issued in that war against flying metal. The other is a long strip of cloth, folded, waiting to be tied. Every morning in the trenches, a Sikh soldier picked up the cloth. When the helmets came, the soldiers were asked to wear them. The accounts from the war say Sikh soldiers kept their turbans and went into the line without the steel. Why would a man in a place where flying metal could kill him choose cloth over steel? The answer starts with the hair underneath.
screen: `A STEEL HELMET.` → `A STRIP OF CLOTH.` → `THEY KEPT THE CLOTH.`

segments.voice: First, the hair. Kesh, uncut hair, is one of the five articles a Khalsa Sikh keeps, along with the comb, the steel bracelet, the short sword and the cotton undergarment. The Sikh code of conduct, the Rehat Maryada, asks Sikhs to keep their hair uncut, as it grew. Second, the turban. The dastar covers and keeps that hair. The code asks Sikh men to wear one, and some Sikh women wear one too. It isn't a hat. A hat comes off at the door. The turban is part of how a Sikh keeps the Guru's form, and it is spoken of as a crown. Third, the helmet. A steel helmet would not sit over a turban, and taking off the turban to fit one would mean setting aside what the code asks a Sikh to wear over uncut hair. So the accounts say the soldiers kept their turbans, and took the danger that came with that. The turban stayed. Fourth, what it says today. A turban can be seen from across a street. It tells everyone who you are before you speak, which is a kind of courage on an ordinary Tuesday, in an office, on a bus, at a school gate. The soldiers wore it into the trenches. Sikhs today tie it before work. That's today's line: the turban stayed.
screen: `KESH: UNCUT HAIR, ONE OF THE FIVE.` · `THE DASTAR KEEPS IT. NOT A HAT.` · `A HELMET WOULDN'T SIT ON IT.` · `SEEN FROM ACROSS THE STREET.` · then, large: `THE TURBAN STAYED.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with who you are. Sit tall, as if something you value were resting on your head. If you wear a turban, a kara, a cross, a scarf, a ring that means something, feel it now: its weight, where it touches you. If you wear nothing like that, think of one thing about you that people can see and that you'd keep even when it costs you: an accent, a name, a habit of kindness. Breathe in, and own it. Breathe out, and let the worry about other people's eyes loosen. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Turbans. The dastar, the cloth that covers and keeps a Sikh's uncut hair, which Sikh soldiers kept on when the steel helmets came. Today's word.
Your line: the turban stayed. Today, wear one thing that says who you are, and wear it without apology. Day nine hundred ninety-eight.

howItsDone: Sikhs who keep their hair uncut tie the dastar each morning; Sikh men wear it as the Rehat Maryada asks, and some Sikh women wear one as well.

Rehat Maryada wording: the code asks Sikhs to keep hair uncut and Sikh men to wear a turban (for women it is optional). Please confirm the paraphrase.
